content: The document discusses the management and regulation of public health pesticides, emphasizing the importance of ensuring their safe and effective use to control vector-borne diseases such as malaria, dengue, leishmaniasis, and Chagas disease. It highlights the reliance on chemical pesticides for vector control and the need to minimize their adverse effects on human and animal health, as well as the environment. The International Code of Conduct on Pesticide Management provides voluntary global standards for the distribution and use of pesticides. However, many countries, particularly those with decentralized health systems or endemic vector-borne diseases, face significant challenges in managing public health pesticides. These challenges include inadequate regulatory frameworks, limited capacity for quality control, and insufficient training and public awareness. The World Health Organization (WHO), with financial support from the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation, implemented a six-year project (2007–2013) to address these issues. The project aimed to reduce health risks associated with pesticides by strengthening national regulatory frameworks, harmonizing registration procedures, improving post-registration monitoring, and reducing the trade of substandard pesticide products. The WHO Pesticide Evaluation Scheme (WHOPES) led the project in collaboration with WHO regional offices and the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO). Key achievements of the project include: 1. Building an Evidence Base: Global surveys were conducted to assess pesticide registration and management practices in countries at risk of vector-borne diseases. 2. Raising Awareness and Political Support: Workshops and consultations were held to sensitize policymakers and program managers about the critical need for sound pesticide management. These events encouraged countries to develop national policies and allocate budgets for pesticide management. 3. Developing Guidelines and Standards: Authoritative guidelines on pesticide registration, management, efficacy testing, and risk assessment were developed through international expert consultations. These guidelines aim to harmonize procedures and improve pesticide management globally. 4. Providing Technical Support and Training: Priority countries received technical support to assess their pesticide management practices, develop national action plans, and strengthen laboratory capacity for quality control. Training was provided to regulatory authorities and national staff on developing quality standards and evaluating pesticide equivalence. 5. Expanding the WHOPES Network: The global network of WHO Collaborating Centres and partner institutions was expanded to enhance capacity for testing and evaluating public health pesticides. These institutions serve as centers of excellence for pesticide evaluation. The project also highlighted the increasing global use of pyrethroids for vector control, raising concerns about the potential development of resistance. Additionally, the continued use of DDT despite the Stockholm Convention underscores the need for effective pesticide resistance management. The document emphasizes the importance of investing in infrastructure, equipment, and training to enable full quality control of pesticides in line with FAO/WHO specifications. It also calls for the inclusion of public health pesticides in national legislation and the establishment of functional quality control laboratories. Overall, the project underscores the need for coordinated efforts, evidence-based strategies, and international collaboration to improve the management of public health pesticides and reduce the burden of vector-borne diseases.
